sections.title: From Concrete to Abstract: The Shift
sections.content: Briefly revisit 2D vectors (arrows in a plane). Introduce the concept of abstraction: stripping away the geometry to focus on the 'rules' of interaction (addition and scaling).
sections.example: Comparing a physical arrow on a grid to a set of 'recipes' for mixing colors or scheduling tasks.

sections.title: The Eight Axioms: Defining the Playground
sections.content: Introduce the formal structure of a vector space (V, + , ·). Focus on the core pillars: Closure, Associativity, Commutativity, Identity, and Distributivity.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Robot's Instruction Set': If we can combine two sets of instructions (vector addition) and speed them up (scalar multiplication), do they still result in a valid instruction?

sections.title: Non-Geometric Vectors
sections.content: Demonstrate that 'vectors' aren't just arrows. Show how polynomials or functional data can satisfy the same algebraic rules, expanding the learner's intuition.
sections.example: Representing a 'Polynomial' as a vector: P(x) = ax² + bx + c becomes the vector (a, b, c). Adding two polynomials is just vector addition.

sections.title: Synthesis & The Universal Framework
sections.content: Concluding the 5-minute session by showing that since these entities follow the same axioms, we can use the same linear algebra theorems (like bases and dimensions) on all of them.
sections.example: A 'Chef's Toolkit': Whether the 'vector' is a list of ingredients or a set of cooking temperatures, the logic of scaling and combining remains identical across domains.

storyboard.title: From Concrete to Abstract: The Shift
lecture_lines: Vectors are more than just arrows in space.
We strip away geometry for abstract rules.
Focus on addition and scalar scaling.
Think of recipes for mixing colors.
Or complex tasks scheduled over time.
